blocks.title: Decide what goes where before a single bed gets cut.
body: Landscape design is a plan for the whole property: where the beds go, which plants go in them, how the stone and edges run, and how water gets away from the house. HD Landscape plans all of that around your yard, then builds it.

Most yards were never planned. A shrub went in here, a bed got cut there, and twenty years later nothing lines up. A design looks at everything at once, so you do not end up paying to redo the same corner twice.

blocks.title: The yard decides most of the plan.
blocks.intro: A good design starts with what is already there. We read these on the walk, and each one changes the plan.

items.title: Sun and shade
items.body: Plants do not read the tag. We look at how much sun each bed actually gets, after the house and the big trees take their share, and choose from there.

items.title: Water and grade
items.body: Clay is common across Metro Detroit, and it holds water. If the ground slopes the wrong way, no plant choice will save it, so [yard grading](/yard-grading/) goes in the plan first.

items.title: Full grown size
items.body: Small shrubs set close to the house are the classic mistake. They look tidy the day they go in, then spend the next decade pressing against the siding. Leave room for the plant it will become.

items.title: Road salt and snow
items.body: Beds along a drive or street take salt and plowed snow all winter. Purdue Extension rates eastern white pine as sensitive to salt spray, so it belongs back from the salted edge.

items.title: Big trees
items.body: Big trees usually stay, and the plan works around them. MSU Extension says about 80 percent of a tree's roots sit in the top 18 to 24 inches of soil, so soil should not get piled over them to make a bed or a flat lawn. A big tree that has to come down is a job for a tree company, not our crew.

items.title: All four seasons
items.body: A yard should still look like something in January. Evergreens, stone and clean bed lines carry the winter, and flowers and fall color get layered in around them.

blocks.title: Pick the bed before we dig it.
blocks.intro: Mulch or stone, dark or light. The bed material sets the look of the whole yard, so try the options here and tell Jake which one suits your house.

It suits people who want one company on it from the first walk to the last rake. If you are after a drawing to put out for bids, tell Jake that on the walk, so you both know where you stand.

blocks.title: In St. Clair Shores, **start with the water.**
blocks.intro: St. Clair Shores is home base for HD Landscape, on the west side of Lake St. Clair. Zoning allows one family lots from 6,000 square feet inland, and lakeshore districts start at 20,000, so the same plan rarely suits both.

items.title: Small lots that show everything
items.body: On a small lot, every foot of the front bed counts. A few well placed plants and one clean bed line usually do more than a solid row of shrubs.

items.title: Clay that holds water
items.body: USDA soil maps put poorly drained clay loams across most of the city, on ground with very little slope. So the plan starts with where the water will go, raised beds can make sense in the wet spots, and plant choices come after that.

items.title: Yards near the water
items.body: The city has 14 miles of canals, and those yards and the lakefront take the wind off Lake St. Clair. High water flooded parts of town in 2019 and 2020, so a plan here should allow for wet ground and keep the view of the water open.

items.title: Ask the city before moving dirt
items.body: Michigan generally requires a soil erosion permit for earth changes within 500 feet of a lake or stream, and St. Clair Shores runs that program itself, not the county. Ask early, so the plan you fall in love with is one you can build.

faq.q: Do you do landscape design in St. Clair Shores?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape designs and builds yards in St. Clair Shores, MI, where the company is based and works often. Most of the city sits on slow draining clay, so a plan here usually deals with the water first. We also work across Metro Detroit, including [Grosse Pointe](/landscape-design-grosse-pointe-mi/), [Birmingham](/landscape-design-birmingham-mi/), [Bloomfield Hills](/landscape-design-bloomfield-hills-mi/) and [Rochester](/landscape-design-rochester-mi/). Call or text Jake at [(586) 718-8762](tel:+15867188762).

faq.q: What does a landscape design include?
faq.a: A landscape design from HD Landscape covers the layout of your beds, the plants, the stone and edging, and how water leaves the yard. It starts with Jake on the property with you, because what works depends on the yard in front of him. Our crew then builds it, and the estimate lists each part on its own line.

The estimate from HD Landscape is free. For a full design, ask Jake how it is handled when he sees the yard, before any planning starts. Our plans are made for our own crew to build, so the plan and the build go together.

faq.q: How much does a landscape design project cost?
faq.a: The yard sets the number: how big it is, how much the grade has to change and what goes in. Two yards the same size can land far apart if one needs grading first. Jake prices it once he has seen it, and there is no charge for the estimate. It comes itemized, so every piece of the plan has its own line.

faq.q: Do you build the landscape you design?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape plans the job and our crew builds it, so one company is on it from the first walk to the follow-up call. Jake also calls after the crew is done to check how it went and go over watering.

faq.q: How long does landscape design take?
faq.a: A front bed and a full property are very different jobs, so Jake can give you a clear idea once he has seen the yard. On the build side, some jobs wrap up in a day and bigger ones take longer.

faq.q: When should I start planning a new landscape in Michigan?
faq.a: Start before the season you want it built, because the plan comes before any ground work. We work in Michigan while the ground is workable. For new trees, the Michigan DNR recommends spring or fall, and Michigan State University Extension leans toward spring because new roots stall as the soil cools.

faq.q: Can you design a landscape for clay soil?
faq.a: Yes. Clay is common in southeast Michigan and drains slowly, so the plan deals with drainage first and plants go in at the right depth. The Michigan DNR says a tree's root flare should sit level with the top of the hole or slightly above it.

faq.q: Do you design low maintenance landscapes?
faq.a: Yes, if that is what you want. Low maintenance mostly comes from the right plant in the right spot, with room for its full grown size, so you are not cutting it back every year. [Monthly landscape maintenance](/monthly-landscape-maintenance/) is there for upkeep you would rather hand off, and what a visit covers is set on your estimate.

faq.q: Can you design just my front yard?
faq.a: Yes. A front yard or a single problem area is a fine place to start. Jake will look at how it connects to the rest of the property, so a later phase does not mean undoing this one.

faq.q: Do you install sprinklers as part of a landscape design?
faq.a: No. HD Landscape does not install sprinkler systems. If you want one, have it put in before the planting, and we will plant around it. New plants still need steady water, and we offer [plant watering](/plant-watering/) while they settle in.
Yes. We work on residential and commercial properties. Entry beds, planters, hedges and stone along a building get planned the same way as a home, with the same itemized estimate.
